title: George Bonanno's The End of Trauma and Notes on Trauma Informed
author: Lemov, Doug
summary: The words "trauma" and "trauma informed" get used a lot these days in and around schools and some of the uses give me pause. For example they tend to assume that any young person who has been through a horrible experience is traumatized. But this is not true and the unsystematic use of diagnoses erodes our ability to recognize and respond to students who really have undergone real trauma. Further, without understanding of why some people are traumatized, why others aren't, and how people get over trauma we've at real risk of taking well-intentioned actions that are counter-productive both to students who may be traumatize and the larger population of students who aren't In light of that I'd like to strongly recommend George Bonanno's book, The End of Trauma: How the New Science of Resilience Is Changing How We Think About PTSD Bonanno is a Professor of Clinical Psychology and Chair of the Department of Counseling and Clinical Psychology at Columbia University's Teachers College and one of the leading experts on trauma. Summary: Bonanno defines Trauma as negative experiences outside the frame of normal human experience. PTSD he argues, even in the worst cases, is relatively rare. Most people, even when the most awful things happen, are ultimately ok. Difficulty, even extreme difficulty, is normal and so is the struggle to come to terms with brutal experiences. But experiencing these things and overcoming them is a central part of human experience. PTSD is when things don't go away ... when months after a person still experiences intrusive thoughts and cannot return to normalcy. Bonanno's argues that there are no traumatic events. There are only "potentially traumatic events"- that no matter how bad, terrible events are not traumatic for most people. Yes, they may struggle. But no matter how bad the event, most people return to normalcy within a reasonable period of time. That said, even the 'normal' struggle to overcome awful events is critical to understand, and in fact this is one of his key points. Previously most Trauma research was really writing that came from a clinical perspective, i.ee it studied people who HAD adverse reactions. Bonanno wants to study the totality of reactions--including especially people who recover successfully--and he outlines what we know about the process by summarizing the resilience trajectory (what we know about the path most people take back to coping) and flexibility mindset- which is the successful mental habits that correlate to and are most likely to result in healthy responses to the worst psychological situations. While we know certain things about what helps people cope the strength of the signal is low. There's a lot we don't understand and no clear recipe. One of Bonanno's themes is that any trait or behavior always has a benefit and a cost; an upside and a downside so the key is a flexibility mind set. Choosing the right tool to become resilient in response to an anomalous situation that is outside the frame of normal experience. The "solution" such as it is for getting on a resilience trajectory is a flexibility mindset. It consists of optimism, confidence and challenge orientation. These are not traits but actions and skills. Some people are better at them and more inclined to use them under duress (small duress or large duress) but anyone can do them to some degree. [One of my key takeaways is that schools should constantly be building the elements of the flexibility mindset to enable people to get n the resilience pathway. That means building optimism confidence and a challenge receptivity in students. and in fact schools are good places because they are built over time and synergize with other aspect of our mission.] Another takeaway is that we should use the word trauma cautiously. Telling students they have been through trauma makes the hill larger and telling ourselves they are traumatized inclines us to treat them as fragile when part of what they need is for us to remind them that they can get through. We should help them to build optimism, confidence and receptivity to challenge. They need to believe they are capable. Here are some of my notes from his book [italics mostly mine]: "Research over the past several decades has shown incontrovertibly that most people exposed to violent or life-threatening events do not develop PTSD. And that can only mean that these events are not inherently traumatic. No event, not even a violent or life-threatening event, is inherently traumatic. Such events are only "potentially traumatic." ... Most people exposed to potentially traumatic events are able to continue on with their normal lives relatively quickly and without suffering any long-term difficulties. In short most people are resilient." (14) "I call this the resilience paradox. We can identify statistical correlates of resilience--the so called traits of resilient people-but paradoxically when something aversive happens these correlates don't actually tell us much about who will be resilient and who not." (15) Flexibility: "Even traits and behaviors that seem most obviously useful--say, expressing emotion, or seeking support from others--aren't universally helpful. and in some situations traits and behaviors that we typically think of as problematic such as suppressing emotion, are exactly what we need. This means, effectively, that we have to work out the best solution moment by moment as we struggle and then we have to readjust as we go along. In other words we have to be flexible....[but] flexibility is not a passive process. We need what I call the flexibility mindset." (16) "Psychological problems don't lend themselves well to a disease model. There is no clear pathogen or biological event that causes most mental disorders, including PTSD, and there is no physical test that can confirm its existence...They are essentially invented by committee." (36-37) "By introducing subjectivity into the definition the criteria became so ambiguous that practically anything extremely unpleasant could qualify as trauma." (38) [Be careful of "conceptual bracket creep" that has the effect of] "moving the PTSD diagnosis a step closer to becoming meaningless." "One of the pioneers of this research, Ann Masten, perhaps put it best: 'The biggest surprise that emerged from the study of children who overcome adversity... was the ordinariness of the phenomenon.' To describe the commonplace nature of childhood adaptation to hardship she coined the beautifully poetic phrase ordinary magic." (43) [Post 9/11 NYC braced for massive waves of psychological problems that did not emerge.] "Patricia Resnick, a renowned trauma researcher...did not mince words: "People's expectations about the impact of the attack on the country's mental health were wrong," she wrote. "Lesson? Strong emotions do not equal psychopathology." The resilience trajectory: "When people in otherwise normal circumstances are exposed to an isolated and potentially highly disruptive event but nonetheless maintain "a stable trajectory of healthy functioning across time." "weak severity effects" [very low correlation between the severity of the trauma and the emotional level of the response in the potential patient]. "There are other characteristics that have been shown to have an empirical relationship to resilience. One of the best known is support from other people. Another is optimism and relatedly, the belief in one's ability to cope well. People showing resilient outcomes also tend not to search for meaning after potential trauma but rather to focus on problem solving. They are able to use a range of coping and emotion regulation strategies... "Coping and emotion regulation strategies are inherently neither good nor bad. Every strategy is effective only insofar as it helps us meet the demands of a specific situation....The leading theorists on coping and emotion regulation have always emphasized this kind of dynamic interaction with changing situational demands." ... I have called this "Pragmatic coping" or "coping ugly" a lot of trial and error. (105) "Traits and behaviors that correlate with resilience show pretty modest effects and this is largely because no one trait or behavior is always useful. Every behavior and every trait comes with both benefits and costs." (118) "Flexibility is not resilience. It is the process we use to adapt ourselves to traumatic stress so that we can find our way to resilience." (121) Flexibility does not simply happen. it is not a passive process. Although we often represent the idea of flexibility with images of some sort of pliable material such as rubber or bamboo that passively bends with pressure humans do not simply bend. We bend ourselves. That process takes at least some effort and engagement with the task at hand." (122) "The flexibility mindset is essentially a conviction that we will be able to adapt ourselves to the challenge at hand, that we will do whatever is needed to move forward. At the core of the mindset are three interrelated beliefs: optimism about the future, confidence in our ability to cope and a willingness to think about threat as a challenge.... These beliefs interact and complement each other in a way that multiplies their individual impact. And collectively they produce a robust conviction, a mindset that says in effect..."I will find a way to deal with this challenge." (123) "Stress hardiness" is "an intermediate step, a collection of beliefs that [Kobasaa et al] "provides the courage and motivation to do the hard work of turning stressful circumstances from potential disasters into growth opportunities." This set of beliefs they aid creates a "pathway" that can eventually lead to resilience." (125) "Optimism is defined as a general belief that the future will turn out well, even when there is no particular evidence that this is likely to be the case. In other words, optimism is a bias, an interpretation of possible futures that is tilted towards the positive. Not surprisingly some people are reliably more optimistic than others. But almost everyone is capable ofbeing optimistic at least some of the time." (127) "Optimism, measured years before a potentially traumatic event, predicted a resilience trajectory once that event occurred." (128) [DL Note: The optimism is best when it exists always... in advance of difficulty... we should be always building it in schools] [DL Note: The resilience trajectory applies no matter what the setback. It's our best bet for young people who are resilient in the face of PTEs but also who overcome adversity more generally] "The results of this study showed that resilient survivors had all the ingredients of a flexibility mindset. They were optimistic, the saw themselves as efficacious copers, and they were focused on the challenges that lay before them.... confidence in coping motivates in a different way from optimism. It can give us that little extra push to be more adventurous. When we feel confident that we can handle ourselves we will likely try a broader range of behaviors. We might even try behaviors we are not sure we are able to do, simply because we assume ourselves likely to succeed. And like optimism this kind of confidence becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. People who view themselves as effective copers don't just think they cope better; on the whole they actually do cope better, both with current stressors and with whatever stressors they might encounter in the future." (145) [DL Note: Tou build up feelings of efficaciousness by overcoming small hurdles again and again. Success motivates and informs in other words which is why a schools teaching and its willingness to push and challenge students in a loving way is, we believe, tied to the mental resilience of its students... you build up a habit of seeing things that you think will be challenging and then overcoming them. easy is not better. but success is important. this is because "what we are able to do depends on the kinds of tools we have at our disposal, our repertoire" (170). [The tools are built in advance... or at least made available by other, analogous experiences] "When we shift our focus to the challenges [and away from the problem or "threat] things begin to happen. For starters we take a more active stance and we begin to think about the stressor differently we see it less as a threat to endure and more as a challenge to be met." (146) "The orientation toward challenge becomes even more crucial when stressors persist over longer periods of time. For example, children who are bullied in school but interpret the situation as a challenge have been found to be more likely to seek help and thus are more likely to overcome these experiences." In case you want more, the book should be required reading for anyone who uses the term "trauma-informed." You can also listen to my interview with George Bonanno here. He's quite critical of many of the things that are done under the rubric of "trauma informed."
